h1: Landscaping and acreage care in Metchosin
cardSummary: Farms, forest and shoreline, where streams and wetlands can bring provincial riparian rules into garden plans.
intro: Metchosin is farms, forest and shoreline: rural acreages through Happy Valley, waterfront around Witty’s Lagoon and William Head, and wooded lots toward Rocky Point.

The District regulates tree removal under its Tree Management Bylaw and asks owners to call the Municipal Hall before removing trees. Where a stream or wetland is on or next to a property, the BC Riparian Areas Regulation may also apply. See [tree and vegetation work](/services/tree-vegetation/) or [get a free quote](/free-quote/?area=metchosin).
localRulesIntro: Metchosin’s first step is simple: call the Municipal Hall before removing trees. Streams, wetlands and the lagoon also bring in provincial riparian rules, which matter for clearing and new beds near water.

localNotes.title: Metchosin Tree Management Bylaw
localNotes.text: Metchosin's Tree Management Bylaw regulates tree removal; the District asks owners to call the Municipal Hall before removing trees. Where a stream or wetland is on or next to the property, the BC Riparian Areas Regulation may also apply.

localNotes.title: CRD lawn-watering schedule (connected properties only)
localNotes.text: CRD Stage 1 watering rules run May 1 to September 30 for properties on the regional water supply (many rural properties use wells; the rules apply only where connected): lawns may be watered on Wednesdays and Saturdays (even addresses) or Thursdays and Sundays (odd addresses), 4-10 am or 7-10 pm; hand watering and drip irrigation of trees, shrubs and gardens is allowed any day. Multi-unit complexes use the complex's street address. New sod or seed does not need a permit and has a temporary schedule.

localNotes.title: Invasive plants and disposal
localNotes.text: The CRD Regional Invasive Species Program lists priority species (including giant hogweed, knotweed, gorse, poison hemlock, shiny geranium and yellow toadflax) and asks for sightings to be reported. Invasive plants must be disposed of properly: Hartland Landfill takes them bagged and labelled or in covered loads, and knotweed needs a controlled waste permit and is not accepted at municipal yard-waste drop-offs.

conditions.title: Streams, wetlands and the lagoon
conditions.body: Many lots have a creek, ditch or wet area. Clearing and new planting near water are kept back and planned with the riparian rules in mind.

conditions.title: Field edges and fence lines
conditions.body: Hayfields, pasture and fence lines fill with broom and blackberry if left. Regular cutting before broom sets seed keeps them open.

conditions.title: Deer and wildlife
conditions.body: Deer are common, so gardens near the house usually need fencing or deer-resistant planting.

conditions.title: Check your water supply
conditions.body: Rural properties may be on wells or on the regional supply. The CRD lawn days apply only where you are connected.

topServices.why: Invasive removal and brush clearing along trails, fields and fence lines are frequent needs on rural lots.
Acreage and farm properties need mowing, hedge and fence-line upkeep through the growing season.

servicesBlurb.grounds-maintenance: Acreage and farm property upkeep: mowing, hedges and fence lines.
servicesBlurb.landscape-installation: Planting and simple hardscape for rural homes.
servicesBlurb.irrigation: Drip and spray systems for gardens on wells or the regional supply.
servicesBlurb.tree-vegetation: Invasive removal, brush clearing and tree work after a check with the District.

jobNotes.title: Broom cut before it seeded
jobNotes.body: Scotch broom along a hayfield fence line was cut in late spring before seed set, and the material was bagged and labelled for proper disposal.

jobNotes.title: New beds kept back from a creek
jobNotes.body: New garden beds were laid out well back from a seasonal creek, with the plan discussed with the District before any vegetation came out.
